item.title: The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide

Submitted by Sondos Asem on Fri, 10/16/2026 - 08:00
Judges in the Gambia v Myanmar case are preparing a ruling that will have ramifications for Israel and Gaza

In the first week of September 2017, Antonia Mulvey was on the Bangladesh-Myanmar border, interviewing women and children who had fled across it days earlier.

“Women waited all day to talk to me and they'd had horrific things happen to them,” she told Middle East Eye. “What struck me when I listened to their stories was that they were asking me for justice.”

Mulvey was one of the first three investigators deployed by a UN fact-finding mission. Her brief was sexual violence and crimes against children.

Nine years later, the case that grew out of those accounts is nearing its end, with the International Court of Justice (ICJ) expected to rule in the coming weeks on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Mulvey, now executive director of Legal Action Worldwide (LAW), which represents Rohingya witnesses in the case, said that if the judges rule against Myanmar, it will be the first time the court has found a state responsible for committing genocide.

For many Rohingya, the ruling is about more than the past. “We need to fix the root cause,” one refugee told LAW researchers. “The best justice for us is to fix the root cause of the problem.”

Decades of persecution

The Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority, have lived for generations in western Myanmar’s Rakhine State. Northern Rakhine was the only part of the country where they formed a majority.

Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law left the Rohingya off the list of the country's officially recognised ethnic groups, leaving most of them stateless. 

The state and its lawyers refer to the Rohingya as “Bengalis”, a term that casts them as migrants from Bangladesh.

For decades, restrictions on the Rohingya’s movement, marriage rights, education and access to healthcare have been documented. Hundreds of thousands fled to Bangladesh in waves of violence in 1978, and again in 1991 and 1992. 

In 2012, clashes in Rakhine displaced about 140,000 people, most of them Rohingya. Many remain confined to camps around the state capital, Sittwe. 

“Rohingya have been persecuted in Myanmar for decades,” said Salma, a Rohingya survivor who attended the ICJ hearings in January, in comments shared by LAW. She asked that only her first name be used.

For many refugees, justice now means one thing above all: citizenship. In a survey conducted by LAW of just under 500 refugees in the Cox's Bazar camps in Bangladesh, 86 percent of participants said citizenship and the right to identify as Rohingya were necessary for justice. 

“We want [the] international community to destroy the 1982 law, and we hope they will do it,” one participant said. “We had Myanmar citizenship, and we were living there for a long time, and our citizenship should be restored. If they provide these two things, we will get everything.”

“They want justice, but they want citizenship,” Mulvey said. “They want to be acknowledged for what happened, and they want that land and property back.”

'Clearance operations'

On 25 August 2017, Myanmar's military launched what it called “clearance operations” in northern Rakhine State, after the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) attacked police posts. 

More than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh in the months that followed. About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in the camps of Cox's Bazar.

In 2018, the UN fact-finding mission concluded that there was enough information to infer genocidal intent. It called for senior generals - including then-army chief Min Aung Hlaing, who is now president - to be investigated and prosecuted. 

Mulvey said she drafted the report's sections on sexual violence and crimes against children.

“It was the UN fact-finding mission report that Gambia relied upon in order to initiate proceedings at the ICJ,” she said. 

Abubacarr Tambadou, the Gambia's then justice minister, had spent years as a prosecutor at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. He visited the Cox's Bazar camps in 2018. 

In November 2019, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, the Gambia filed its case.

The West African country had no direct link to the violence. It relied on the principle, accepted by the court in 2022, that every state party to 1948's Genocide Convention has a common interest in seeing it upheld.

In January 2020, the court unanimously ordered Myanmar to take all measures within its power to prevent genocidal acts. 

A year later, the military seized power. 

In July 2022, the judges rejected Myanmar's objections to the court's jurisdiction, clearing the way for the hearings that took place in January this year.

'We have never heard evidence like this'

Over three weeks of hearings, the court heard from three Rohingya witnesses in closed session: two men and a woman. They were identified in court only by their initials, and each came from one of three villages at the centre of The Gambia's case: Min Gyi, Maung Nu and Chut Pyin.

Mulvey, their lawyer, said they spoke about the killing of their family members, the sexual violence they had been subjected to and their flight from Rakhine. Two travelled to the Hague from Cox's Bazar and one from Canada, where they had been resettled.

“It was very silent. You could also hear crying. It was extraordinarily powerful testimony,” Mulvey said. “Of course we have to wait to see what the judgment is, but you could feel the weight of it.”

She said court staff told her: “We have never heard evidence like this ever in the court.”

LAW also brought a victims' delegation of three Rohingya survivors to sit in the courtroom: a man, a woman and a hijra, a term used in South Asia for transgender and intersex people. 

Mulvey said it was the first time a transgender person had been seen in the court.

“We did not know that legal proceedings existed, and we could fight for our rights,” Salma, who part of the delegation, said. “But this time, we have the tools to defend ourselves and demand accountability and reparation for what happened to us.” 

Rehana, the delegation's hijra member, who also asked to be identified by her first name only, said she hoped a ruling would include the whole community. “If the genocide is recognised, we hope that we will be getting our justice. Justice for our entire community, including hijra,” she said.

LAW also submitted hundreds of pages of written witness evidence, which Mulvey said The Gambia relied on heavily.

Rape and sexual violence were central to The Gambia's case. “They selected, particularly, women and girls of reproductive age. They gang raped them. That was the method of choice,” Mulvey said, of army soldiers. 

She said investigators found “a pattern of biting, to leave an indelible mark on them”. She said rape in front of the community reflected “the intent to destroy the very social fabric of the community”.

The ICJ has accepted before that rape can be an act of genocide, in Bosnia v Serbia and Croatia v Serbia. But in neither case did it find the intent required to classify those acts as genocide.

A ruling against Myanmar on this point would mark “the first time the ICJ has actually found sexual violence itself to constitute genocide in a merits judgment”, Mulvey said.

What is genocide?

In deciding the case, the judges will draw on the Genocide Convention itself, the court’s own earlier rulings, and the case law of the international criminal tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda.

Israel’s war on Gaza: What is the meaning of genocide?
Read More »

The Genocide Convention, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948, defines genocide as any of five acts “committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such”. 

In Bosnia v Serbia in 2007, the court held that the intent must be to destroy at least a substantial part of the group, and that it must be physical or biological destruction rather than cultural destruction. 

It also ruled that charges of such exceptional gravity against a state must be proved by evidence that is “fully conclusive”.

Intent can be shown by “particular circumstances” or inferred from a pattern of conduct. But in Croatia v Serbia in 2015, the court set a high bar for inference. To infer genocidal intent from a pattern of conduct, it said, “it is necessary and sufficient that this is the only inference that could reasonably be drawn from the acts in question”.

Applying those tests, the court found in 2007 that genocide had been committed only at Srebrenica, and that Serbia was responsible for failing to prevent and punish it, not for committing it. 

The Gambia's case

Philippe Sands and Paul Reichler, two lawyers representing the Gambia, argued that Myanmar’s military operations in northern Rakhine State targeted a substantial part of the Rohingya population and that the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy the group.

Sands used Myanmar's own figures from its written pleadings to address whether Myanmar had targeted a “substantial” part of the Rohingya.

'They selected, particularly, women and girls of reproductive age. They gang raped them. That was the method of choice'

- Antonia Mulvey, lawyer

He calculated that 815,459 Rohingya lived in northern Rakhine's three townships, Maungdaw, Buthidaung and Rathedaung, before the 2017 operations. About 700,000 of them, nearly nine in 10, fled to Bangladesh. The military “targeted tens of thousands of homes, and over 800,000 human beings”, Sands said.

Myanmar had argued that the estimated 10,000 to 25,000 people killed did not amount to a substantial part of the group. Sands said those figures were “likely to be an underestimate”. 

Myanmar “has gone out of its way to destroy the evidence, including the evidence of the burial of large numbers of bodies in mass graves”, he said.

“Genocide is not a numbers game,” Sands said, explaining that “there is no magical number of victims which turns one kind of crime into another kind of crime”.

“The 700,000 who fled to Bangladesh for their lives were no less targeted than their murdered brothers and sisters,” the British lawyer said.

Sands also argued that northern Rakhine mattered because it was the one region where Rohingya were the majority. 

Turning to intent, he said that it was proved both by “particular circumstances” and by a pattern of conduct. He pointed first to the three witnesses' villages.

“There is no world in which the shooting of Witness MS's daughter, as she waded across a river to escape, was not genocidal; or the intentional burning of his wife and four other children inside a house,” Sands told the court. 

“There is no world in which the gang rape of Witness NJ, the murder of her infant child in front of her, was not genocidal.”

Myanmar acted with genocidal intent, Sands said, because “its discriminatory policies, its hate speech, its pre-planning and organisation, its extreme brutality, its sexual violence, its targeting of children, its destruction of evidence, its impunity for the perpetrators, its failure to co-operate with the UN, cannot reasonably be understood in any other way”.

The counter-terrorism defence

Reichler addressed what is known as the “only reasonable inference” test, which in this case would require proving whether any explanation other than genocide could reasonably account for what happened in Rakhine.

Myanmar's answer was counter-terrorism. “They have put all their eggs in the counter-terrorism basket,” Reichler said.

He told the court that Myanmar's lead counsel, Christopher Staker, had conceded that genocide can take place during a counter-terrorism operation. 

Even if Myanmar was responding to Arsa, he argued, “the fact that there was a counter-terrorism operation in progress … is pure context. It is not intent.”

The question, Reichler said, was what the state intended “at the time its authorised agents began firing their weapons deliberately at Rohingya civilians, including women and children”.

Reichler then dealt with the other possible explanation: that Myanmar meant to drive the Rohingya out, not destroy them. That was the conclusion the court reached about Serbia and Croatia in 2015.

Reichler cited the testimony of the Gambia’s military expert, who was asked whether the operations could have been ethnic cleansing, rather than genocide. The expert said they could not, because ethnic cleansing does not involve killing a group’s children. 

He added that a force seeking only to drive a population out would not keep shooting at people as they fled, or station troops on the river to sink their boats as they were about to reach Bangladesh.

Soldiers also laid landmines at border crossings after 25 August 2017. The fact finding mission said this showed the mines were “intended to target fleeing Rohingya civilians and to prevent those who had already left from returning”.

Russia, Georgia and forced displacement

Reichler contrasted Rakhine with Georgia v Russia, a case in which he had acted for Georgia. 

In this case, Russian forces ordered ethnic Georgians to leave South Ossetia. Those who complied were not harmed. Fleeing refugees were not shot at and there was no systematic sexual violence. “On those facts, if proven, this was forced displacement, or ethnic cleansing. It was not genocide,” Reichler said.

The wars in the former Yugoslavia, he argued, were “essentially about the control of territory”. The Tatmadaw, Myanmar's military, “were not seeking to enlarge Myanmar's territory”.

He warned that Myanmar might “change its narrative in the second round, after we have finished speaking and there is no opportunity for us to respond further”.

Mulvey said that is what happened. Myanmar “did not argue deportation, forcible transfer, only until the very, very, very end of their oral hearings”, she told MEE.

Even if expulsion had been the aim, Reichler argued, the court's own judgments allowed for a genocide finding if the displacement was carried out “with a view to the destruction of the group, as distinct from its removal from the region”.

Reichler argued that other motives, such as fighting Arsa, would not rule out genocidal intent. He noted that in Bosnia the court found genocide at Srebrenica even though the Bosnian Serb leadership's “essential motive” was to create a larger Serb state.

Srebrenica genocide survivors draw parallels with Gaza 30 years after massacre
Read More »

What mattered was the intent at the moment soldiers were “segregating and executing men and boys, raping and gang raping women and girls, killing children and infants – tossing them into fires”. 

He said the destruction continued well into 2018, including in more than 180 villages where Myanmar admits there was no Arsa activity, and was followed by bulldozing, resettlement by ethnic Rakhine and the building of military bases.

Mulvey described the same pattern from her own investigations. 

“They would surround the village. Then often in the early hours of the morning when people were asleep, they would fire mortars into the village. They would then proceed by shooting indiscriminately at civilians,” she told MEE.

She said soldiers continued to shoot at people as they fled towards Bangladesh. “What they did was to ensure that they were killed along the way,” she said.

Myanmar rejected all the allegations. It argued that the operations were a lawful response to attacks by Arsa.

What western nations argued

In November 2023, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the UK filed a joint submission to the court in support of the Gambia. 

They were among 11 states that intervened in the case. States that intervene in this way do not comment on the facts, only on how the Genocide Convention should be read.

The six states warned that the “only reasonable inference” test should not be applied so strictly that genocide becomes “near-impossible” to prove, since states rarely put an intent to destroy a group in writing. 

They also argued that the number of people killed should not decide whether genocide took place. Rape, sexual violence and the targeting of children serve no military purpose, so such acts can point strongly to an intent to destroy a group, they wrote. 

The six states added that UN fact-finding reports deserve particular weight as the work of independent investigators.

Both Sands and Reichler cited the submission in their closing arguments.

'Major repercussions for Israel case'

Michael Becker, a professor of international law at Trinity College Dublin, said this was the first time a court would rule on mass human rights violations in a case brought by “a non-injured state acting to uphold international law”.

“Cases like The Gambia v Myanmar have arguably sought to transform the role and function of the ICJ in contemporary affairs. The outcome here may determine whether that trend will continue,” Becker told MEE.

'Whether the ICJ accepts or rejects that view of genocidal intent will have major repercussions for South Africa's case against Israel'

- Michael Becker, law professor

He said the judgment would be “a crucial opportunity for the ICJ to clarify and develop the law on genocide”, particularly on how intent can be established by inference.

“The core of Myanmar's argument is that actions that can reasonably be characterised as a counter-terrorism operation cannot simultaneously be treated as acts of genocide,” he said.

“Whether the ICJ accepts or rejects that view of genocidal intent will have major repercussions for South Africa's case against Israel at the ICJ, where Israel has similarly claimed that an armed conflict with Hamas precludes a finding that Israel has simultaneously undertaken actions aimed at the physical destruction of the Palestinian population of Gaza,” Becker explained.

Becker said “recent claims that the ICJ may end up 'lowering the standard' to establish genocidal intent are misguided because they fail to acknowledge the ambiguities in the ICJ's pronouncements on genocidal intent”.

He added that the ruling would show how the court treats cases built largely on UN inquiry reports. 

“If the ICJ shows a reluctance to credit the findings of such reports, this will send a strong signal to South Africa (and potential litigants in other future cases) about the need to find other ways to support their claims,” he said.

A major UN inquiry last year already concluded that Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza. Its chief investigator, Navi Pillay, who is also the Gambia's ad hoc judge, told MEE at the time that her report used the same legal standard used by the ICJ in determining a finding of genocide and that it would "bear particular probative value and can be relied upon" by the court.

Israel submitted its response to South Africa's case in March. South Africa's reply is due in November 2027.

What the victims want

Mulvey said she is often asked what a ruling would mean for people in Cox's Bazar “who barely have $1 a day”.

“The short answer is yes, it makes a difference to the community,” she said. “It's important for them that the world's highest court recognises what happened to them.”

Many refugees told LAW researchers that compensation and punishment alone would not be enough. “What is the reason for the issue that happened to us? We need to fix the root cause,” one participant in the survey said. “If we want compensation, their punishment, and such things, I don't think we get our justice.”

'For me, justice means truth. It means that perpetrators must be held accountable'

- Samir Sadaf, young Rohingya 

“Justice [meaning citizenship] is important for our children and grandchildren,” one woman who took part in the survey said. “If it prevails, they will have access to education and they will be able to become successful… in Myanmar.”

The Gambia's final submissions reflected some of these demands. It asked the court to order Myanmar to prosecute those responsible and to provide reparations to the victims.

These include safe and dignified return, the restoration of property, the right to identify as Rohingya, and “full and equal citizenship”.

LAW has called for a trust fund for the Rohingya that would be linked to any reparations the court orders.

Samir Sadaf, a young Rohingya man who fled Rakhine as a child, described what justice would mean beyond a court ruling. 

“For me, justice means truth. It means that perpetrators must be held accountable,” he wrote in an article published by LAW. “Where there is justice, there should be safety, equal rights, freedom of movement, and dignity.”

Enforcing the law

ICJ judgments are binding and cannot be appealed, but the court has no means of enforcing them. If a state refuses to comply, the matter can go to the UN Security Council, where China and Russia, both partners of Myanmar's military government, hold vetoes. 

Min Aung Hlaing, who led the 2017 operations, named himself president in April after contested elections.

“While it may prove impossible to enforce such a judgment while Myanmar continues to operate under military rule, compliance with the ICJ judgment may become the price of readmission to the international community,” Becker said.

A ruling that Myanmar breached the convention “can also increase the pressure on third states to disengage from Myanmar until it demonstrates genuine reform”, he said.

Mulvey said LAW's victims' delegation will be in the courtroom when the judgment is read.

Salma, who sat in the court through the January hearings, said the Rohingya would not give up. “We won't go back without justice,” she said.

item.title: India closes down New Delhi park ahead of 'cockroach' movement rally. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Authorities closed a central New Delhi park Friday before a fresh protest seeking the removal of India’s election chief over a voter-roll revision that critics say has disenfranchised millions.

Organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), the campaign has become the focal point of opposition anger over allegations that the revised rolls favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.

The Election Commission of India, which oversees voting in the world’s most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke urged supporters to rally at the capital’s Central Park after two of his colleagues were detained for breaching security barricades at Jantar Mantar, where they had gone to wave the national flag.

Earlier this week, police removed authorisation for Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site.

On Friday, thousands of security personnel were deployed in parts of the city, with yellow-coloured metal barricades put up at key intersections.

Dipke said he was undeterred despite the possibility of being arrested ahead of Friday’s protest.

“Why are you so afraid of cockroaches?” Dipke said.

“I want to tell Narendra Modi that we are not afraid… if waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready,” he said Thursday.

Delhi’s municipal authorities said they were closing the Central Park for two days for “administrative” reasons.

Delhi Police have barred public gatherings around Connaught Place citing concerns about public order and safety.

item.title: Naseem Shah’s long road to fulfilling his promise as Pakistan’s pace spearhead. [ dawn ]
item.description:
In the soft autumn light of Rawalpindi, where the stands once erupted for a boy barely old enough to drive, Naseem Shah returned to the ground that first announced him to the world.

Seven months had passed since injury forced him off the field. When he returned in the opening Twenty20 International against Sri Lanka last week, the ball still left his hand with its familiar menace.

Three wickets for 36 runs in four overs. A first-ball breakthrough. Pace touching the mid-140s. The crowd remembered. So did Pakistan.

Now three months short of his 24th birthday, Naseem has taken 155 wickets in 93 international matches. His tally includes 60 in Tests at an average of 35.13 and 60 in ODIs at 25.91, with a strike rate of 28.3. The figures speak of promise fulfilled in flashes, and of potential still waiting to fully blossom.

“I feel I’m yet to play my peak cricket,” he told PCB Digital this week. “Whatever cricket I’ve played so far, especially Test cricket, I think I lacked a few things.”

The admission carries the weight of a career lived at high velocity. Born in Mayar, Lower Dir, in February 2003, Naseem was thrust into international cricket at 16. His Test debut against Australia in Brisbane in November 2019 came before many of his peers had finished school.

Three months later, on the Rawalpindi pitch that would become part of his legend, he claimed a hat-trick against Bangladesh. At 16 years and 359 days, he became the youngest bowler to achieve the feat in Test cricket.

The country took to the slight teenager who charged in with raw aggression and an action that drew comparisons with the great fast bowlers of the past.

His early years were a whirlwind. He claimed a five-wicket haul against Sri Lanka at 16, followed by consecutive five-fors in ODIs — 5-33 against the Netherlands in August 2022 and 5-57 against New Zealand the following January. He became only the sixth Pakistan bowler to achieve the feat of taking five wickets in consecutive ODI innings.

In white-ball cricket, Naseem appeared a natural — sharp with the new ball, capable of making the old one reverse and increasingly adept at reading a batter’s intentions. Fast bowling, he now reflects, is “all about aggression and smartness”. The two, he believes, must go hand in hand.

Yet the body that produced such pace has repeatedly let him down. A back injury early in his career cost him more than a year, and shoulder problems followed.

The most painful setback came during the 2023 Asia Cup match against India, when he suffered a tendon injury that required surgery. He watched the World Cup from the sidelines as Pakistan’s campaign unfolded without one of its most threatening bowlers.

“You go back to zero whenever you are injured,” he said. “Sometimes it doesn’t even allow you to go for a run, let alone going through the motions of the game. The rehabilitation programme then becomes important. It is also critical how well you understand your body during those times.”

The latest setback came during the Pakistan Super League earlier this year. A back injury, suffered just as he was rediscovering his rhythm, ruled him out of the tournament and kept him away from the national side for seven months.

During that period of rehabilitation, involving early mornings, carefully planned strengthening exercises and mental adjustment, his understanding of fast bowling began to evolve. The teenage firebrand has become a young man who speaks of awareness, match situations and variations beyond raw speed.

“When you are young you know how to bowl fast,” he explained. “But the important thing is to have sense of what you are trying to do. There are many fast bowlers in the world who bowl 140-plus, but they are not consistent. One or two matches and injuries come.”

He has learnt that bowling at 150 kilometres per hour counts for little if runs flow freely and the body breaks down after a handful of matches. Consistency, execution at 70 or 80 per cent of maximum effort and the ability to surprise a batter with a slower ball after a verbal exchange are among the lessons injury has taught him.

In modern white-ball cricket, where pitches often favour batters and the demands of the game require constant innovation, he believes bowlers must continue to evolve.

His return against Sri Lanka offered an encouraging indication of what lies ahead. In the first T20I, he unsettled the top order before finishing the innings with precision.

In the second, although he went wicketless, he conceded only nine runs in his powerplay overs. It was the kind of disciplined spell that can make a difference in a series. Pakistan won the T20I series 2-1, with Naseem playing his part.

His attention is now turning towards the 2027 World Cup in South Africa, where Pakistan are scheduled to begin their campaign against Afghanistan on Oct 8. It would be his first senior World Cup appearance, following the disappointment of missing the 2023 tournament.

He is also part of the squad for the forthcoming ODI tri-series against England and Sri Lanka, another step in his preparations.

In 34 ODIs, he has demonstrated his ability to compete at the highest level. The challenge now is to sustain that performance over time.

“You make a goal,” he said, “and those goals keep changing with injuries and the ups and downs of a career. But I had set a goal that I want to play cricket up to a certain level. I feel my peak cricket is still ahead of me.”

Looking back, he wonders what more he might have achieved with a better understanding of pitches, his own body and the demands of the game. Looking ahead, he sees only the work that remains.

There is something compelling about the journey of the young man from the mountains of Dir. He arrived as a prodigy and has since endured the isolation of rehabilitation that fast bowlers often face.

The setbacks have been real, the absences painful and the scrutiny relentless. Yet the pace remains, the ball still moves, and his understanding of the game has deepened.

The emphasis has shifted from raw speed to longevity and impact. Pakistan need more than occasional explosive spells. They need a bowler who can deliver consistently, series after series, and take responsibility when the stakes are highest.

The 2027 World Cup is no longer a distant prospect. It is a target around which Naseem can build the next phase of his career.

For a country that has watched him rise, fall and return, the hope is that the boy who took a Test hat-trick at 16 will, as a 24-year-old, deliver the sustained excellence his talent has long promised.

The journey continues. Naseem believes his peak is still to come.

item.title: What options does Indian law provide for CEC’s removal?. [ dawn ]
item.description:
AMID growing calls for the resignation of India’s top election official Gyanesh Kumar for alleged voter roll manipulation, a key issue has come to the fore: the process of the chief election commissioner’s appointment, resignation and termination. The campaign to remove Gyanesh Kumar from office began after a newspaper report alleged that he was responsible for removing the names of 130 million voters from India’s electoral rolls — a figure slightly higher than Bangladesh’s entire voting population.

While the Congress Party, India’s “cockroach” youth movement and others demand Kumar’s resignation, which is simple enough, Kumar’s removal from office is a lengthy and complicated affair, similar to the removal of a Supreme Court judge.

Article 324 of the Indian constitution, whi­ch deals with the Election Commission, outlines the procedures for removal of the election chief. Article 324 (5) stipulates that the top election official shall not be removed fr­­om office “except in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court”.

In India, the CEC is appointed under the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023. The CEC is appointed by the president.

The law stipulates that people who are serving or have served in positions equivalent to a secretary to the Indian government will be eligible. They also have to be “persons of integrity, who have knowledge of and experience in management and conduct of elections”. A search committee, led by the law minister, compiles a panel of five persons for consideration of the selection committee.

The election chief and commissioners are subsequently appointed by the president upon the recommendation of this selection committee, which currently consists of the prime minister, who serves as the chair, along with the leader of opposition in Lok Sabha and a minister as nominated by the prime minister.

The law governing their appointment, however, witnessed a significant change in 2023 where the constitution of the selection committee was changed. Earlier, the selection panel consisted of the prime minister, opposition leader and chief justice of India. The top judge was replaced by a union cabinet minister, for which Narendra Modi chose his home minister, Amit Shah.

Critics argue that this change increases executive influence over the appointment process, as two of the three members of the selection committee would be from the ruling party. As for resigning from office, it is a simple procedure where the election chief or any of the commissioners “may, at any time, by writing under his hand addressed to the president, resign his office”.

Removal

The election chief’s removal follows a quasi-judicial procedure in line with the procedure stipulated by the Judges Inquiry Act, 1968. Supreme Court and High Court judges can be removed on two grounds — proven misbehaviour and incapacity. A written notice must be signed by at least 100 members of the Lok Sabha or 50 members of the Rajya Sabha. The Lok Sabha Speaker or Rajya Sabha Chair examines the notice and available information, and decides to admit or refuse the motion.

If admitted, a committee is convened with one Supreme Court judge, one High Court judge and one distinguished legal expert. The election chief will have the right to defend against the allegation as the committee investigates. If the committee concludes that the charges are not proved, the motion is dropped, and the process ends.

If the committee finds that allegations are true, the report is submitted to the parliament. The motion to remove the election chief will have to carry a special majority (two-thirds of voters present and voting) in both houses, in order to pass. If the motion passes both houses, a formal address is presented to the president, who issues the official order of removal.

The election chief, Gyanesh Kumar has denied accusations of manipulating the voter list during an exercise to verify India’s one billion voters.

Published in Dawn, October 16th, 2026

item.title: From Ismat Chughtai to Dhaka airport: Trapped in the moral policing of the 1940s. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The recent incident involving the alleged imposition of “male guardianship” on three adult women at Dhaka’s international airport is deeply troubling.
The three friends were barred from boarding a flight to Kathmandu for a holiday after immigration officials subjected them to intrusive questioning, moral policing, and harassment.
All three had valid passports, visas, and airline tickets, with no known legal or travel restrictions. Yet, immigration officers stopped them at the checkpoint, interrogated them about their personal lives, and ultimately prevented them from travelling.
What kind of archaic moral policing are we practicing to curtail young women’s freedom of movement in the 21st century?
Fortunately, the incident did not go unchallenged. Forced to miss their scheduled flight, the women refused to let the matter rest and are now pursuing legal action.
This kind of social intrusion and incivility brings to mind a short story I read during my school years in the 1970s.
Written in the early 1940s by Ismat Chughtai, one of the subcontinent’s finest Urdu storytellers, the story is titled Ek Shauhar Ki Khatir (All for a Husband). Although written nearly a century ago, its plot bears an unsettling resemblance to the recent incident at Dhaka airport, highlighting how little our society has changed.
Chughtai’s story revolves around a young, educated, unmarried woman who decides to travel alone by train across British India. Despite warnings from friends and relatives that travelling unescorted is dangerous and socially unacceptable, she sets off on her journey.
En route from Jodhpur to Bombay, she encounters passengers from different walks of life who are deeply unsettled by her decision to travel alone. Her fellow passengers, particularly the traditionally-minded women in the carriage, display palpable patriarchal anxiety over her safety, mobility, and lack of a male protector.
Initially, the train compartment was relatively empty. But as more passengers board, her peaceful journey turns into a battle of intrusive questions.
Her fellow travellers immediately begin probing into her personal life: Where is she going -- to her parents’ home or her husband’s? Where is her husband? Why is she travelling alone? When she casually reveals that she is unmarried and is not going to her parents’ home, their suspicion gives way to pity and horror. To the traditional women in the carriage, an unmarried woman of her age travelling alone is a social anomaly that must somehow be corrected.
To escape their scrutiny and navigate their absurd social expectations, the protagonist decides to play along, claiming that she is married. But the interrogation continues.
Her fellow passengers then demand to know how many children she has. Matching the absurdity of their worldview with equally absurd fabrications, she begins spinning increasingly implausible tales.
When one passenger calculates the timeline and questions how she could have had eight children in just four years of marriage, the protagonist retorts that it is entirely possible to have triplets or quadruplets at a time.
Through the seemingly ordinary setting of a moving train compartment, Chughtai brilliantly satirizes society’s attempts to force independent women into rigid domestic roles. The story draws a timeless parallel with the physical and institutional checkpoints women continue to face today.
Nearly a century later, young, unmarried women in our part of the world continue to face the same patriarchal surveillance, restrictions and moral policing.
Consider an incident in May 2013, when a case at Mumbai’s international airport in India attracted widespread public attention. A 21-year-old female student planning to backpack alone across Europe was subjected to an aggressive and intrusive interrogation by an immigration officer who demanded to know why she was travelling alone.
Crossing all professional boundaries, the officer reportedly said that if her parents allowed her to backpack alone, her family background was “questionable.” He also warned her not to “go crying to the embassy” if anything went wrong.
The ensuing public outcry prompted the Bureau of Immigration to remove the officer from frontline duties permanently and introduce mandatory gender-sensitization workshops at major Indian airports.
Yet, here we are in late 2026, witnessing similar allegations of institutional overreach at Dhaka airport. The officers reportedly questioned why the three women were unmarried, why they were travelling without a male guardian, and whether their families had given them “permission” to travel.
They allegedly went so far as to call one woman’s father and subject him to a humiliating conversation. When challenged, the officials reportedly failed to provide any legal explanation or written justification for stopping the women, effectively derailing their trip.
It is heartening that the travellers refused to remain silent. After their initial administrative complaints went unanswered, they filed a writ petition. In late September 2026, a High Court bench issued a rule questioning the legality of the immigration officials’ actions and asking the home secretary and immigration authorities to explain why preventing adult women from travelling on the basis of their marital or guardianship status should not be declared illegal.
Some officials have informally sought to justify such intrusive questioning by citing the risk of human trafficking through air travel. But can egregious moral policing be excused in the name of anti-trafficking measures? Absolutely not.
Anti-trafficking protocols must never be weaponized to justify gender-based discrimination. A legitimate security mandate does not give officials licence to make offensive remarks about women passengers’ attire, scrutinize their personal finances without proper grounds, or change their professional conduct based solely on a passenger’s marital status.
In Ek Shauhar Ki Khatir , the moment the protagonist assumes the socially sanctioned identity of a “wife,” she is suddenly considered safe and acceptable. The episode exposes just how superficial and arbitrary these social boundaries are.
Nearly a century later, we must ask our state institutions: Do officials manning our international borders really expect unmarried women travelling alone to lie about their marital status and invent male guardians simply to clear immigration?
Unless we dismantle this institutionalized moral policing, our state apparatus will remain little different from the regressive, gossiping train compartment of the 1940s: Frozen in time, hostile to progress, and profoundly threatened by the sight of an independent woman.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Reclaiming our right to breathe. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s characterization of Dhaka’s persistent toxic air as a “matter of national shame” is the sort of candid admission we would like to see more of.
Acknowledging that poisoning the air our children breathe is a deep institutional and civic failure is the vital first step toward addressing the challenge.
For years, our capital’s routine ranking at the very top of global hazardous air quality indexes was met by successive administrations with bureaucratic shrugs, passing the blame to seasonal weather pattern changes, or issuing advisory notices which had little to no substance. This has only exacerbated the air pollution crisis we find ourselves in today.
However, recognizing national embarrassment must immediately be followed by aggressive, uncompromising state action.
While we cannot control every factor that contributes to our toxic air quality, the primary culprits behind Dhaka’s suffocating smog are well-documented: Uncoordinated and unmonitored construction projects kicking up dust, thousands of unfit, smoke-belching vehicles plying the roads and highways, and brick kilns operating around the capital’s periphery in complete defiance of laws and environmental regulations.
The result has been a public health disaster costing thousands of lives annually and draining billions from our healthcare economy.
The PM’s call for public officials to go beyond routine "nine-to-five" duties and take ownership of environmental protection must be heeded. The Ministry of Environment, Forest, and Climate Change, alongside other relevant authority bodies, can no longer treat pollution control as an afterthought.
Addressing Dhaka's air quality requires a zero tolerance approach, which begins with those in power actually caring enough to work on it seriously. Words of acknowledgment are a welcome departure from past denial but will prove to be meaningless if the state does not back those words to reclaim our right to breathe.

item.title: Taking a hard stance against construction oversights. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The tragic collapse of roof shuttering at an under-construction municipal building in Pirganj, Rangpur - which claimed the lives of two workers and left several others injured - is yet another incident that shows Bangladesh’s broken construction oversight.
Day after day, day labourers risk their lives on sites where elementary structural safety measures are routinely sacrificed to cut costs and accelerate deadlines. That this fatal disaster occurred on a public municipal site built under the auspices of the local government makes the negligence all the more indefensible, although, regrettably, not surprising.
In the immediate aftermath, law enforcement have detained the municipal secretary of Pirganj. While preliminary administrative detentions signal initial action, we have seen that all too frequently, high-profile construction disasters end with low-level officials or site supervisors scapegoated to appease public outrage, while influential individuals and decision-makers walk away untouched.
A superficial investigation will not suffice, not for this particular incident nor for future ones. We require a rigorous, independent technical probe to uncover the root causes of this collapse.
Law enforcement must ensure that everyone responsible be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law, regardless of their political connections or administrative rank.
This is far from an isolated incident; structural collapses, fallen scaffolding, and unprotected worksites remain a recurring issue across our country. Construction work must not continue to be a death sentence for vulnerable labourers earning daily wages.
We must enforce strict workplace safety standards, conduct site audits, and impose severe criminal penalties on negligence to begin correcting this issue. Until accountability reaches the very top, human lives will continue to be treated as cheap collateral on our building sites.

item.title: Controlling dengue requires a national strategy rooted in One Health. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Dengue in Bangladesh is no longer a temporary or seasonal health inconvenience; it has evolved into a persistent, multi-faceted public health crisis and a heavy burden on the national economy.
According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) dengue dashboard, over 107,000 individuals have been hospitalized, and more than 331 deaths have been officially documented as of October 15, 2026. With approximately 2,000 new patients admitted daily, the strain on the healthcare system is overwhelming.
Major tertiary hospitals in Dhaka and urban hubs are facing severe shortages of hospital beds and intensive care unit (ICU) capacities. Relatives face frantic scrambles for blood platelets, revealing the systemic fragility of urban medical infrastructure.
These alarming conditions highlight a critical truth: Reactive clinical management after people fall ill, paired with ad-hoc vector control drives, cannot control the transmission chain.
What Bangladesh urgently requires is a year-round, evidence-based preventive policy anchored in a coordinated national framework.
The uninterrupted spread of dengue is deeply intertwined with climate change, unplanned rapid urbanization, chronic waterlogging, and inadequate municipal waste management.
Global environmental and epidemiological research demonstrates that climate volatility, characterized by rising mean temperatures, erratic unseasonal precipitation, and elevated atmospheric humidity, dramatically accelerates the breeding cycles and vector efficiency of Aedes mosquitoes.
Under higher ambient temperatures, the duration required for the dengue virus to replicate inside the mosquito and reach its salivary glands, is significantly shortened. Consequently, an infected female Aedes mosquito becomes capable of transmitting the pathogen to human hosts much faster and more frequently within its lifespan.
Concurrently, urban environments proliferate with artificial micro-habitats. Construction sites, poorly designed drainage infrastructure, discarded single-use plastics, and poorly maintained rooftop gardens collect stagnant water, offering ideal breeding conditions.
Relying exclusively on hospital-centred curative care to address what is inherently an environmental and eco-climatic phenomenon is inherently flawed.
For decades, vector control efforts in Bangladesh have remained stubbornly reactive. Intervention plans are typically mobilized only after hospital admissions surge to crisis levels, taking the form of temporary fogging drives or hospital bed expansions.
Yet, such reactive measures fail to answer fundamental operational questions:
Indiscriminate fogging without routine entomological monitoring wastes municipal resources and damages urban ecosystems, killing beneficial non-target insects while accelerating insecticide resistance in Aedes vectors.
Transitioning from reactive fogging to sustainable vector management demands source reduction, routine larvicidal suppression, systematic waste removal, and targeted bio-control methods.
In this complex landscape, the 'One Health' framework offers the most viable path forward. One Health is an integrated, unifying approach that recognizes the intrinsic interdependence of human health, animal health, and the shared environment.
While dengue is not directly transmitted from animals to humans, it is a vector-borne viral disease reliant on the interaction between human hosts, viral pathogens, mosquito vectors, and ambient environmental conditions.
Applying One Health to dengue control means treating vector ecology, climatic dynamics, human mobility, and urban sanitation as a single interconnected ecosystem.
It breaks down traditional administrative silos, bringing together public health physicians, specialists, medical entomologists, environmental scientists, climate researchers, urban planners, and municipal engineers onto a unified operational platform.
The government recently formed a high-level special taskforce comprising representatives across various ministries and authorities to oversee mosquito-borne disease management, a commendable administrative step.
However, to translate policy into measurable health outcomes, this taskforce must move beyond administrative governance and actively embed the One Health framework into its operational core, with entomologists, climate specialists, and One Health practitioners needing to hold direct scientific advisory roles.
Crucially, Bangladesh needs a predictive national early warning and surveillance system that synthesizes real-time meteorological forecasts, rainfall patterns, vector density indices, larval mapping, and clinical hospitalization data.
Analyzing these spatial data streams will allow authorities to forecast outbreak clusters weeks before human cases spike, shifting intervention efforts from reactive crisis management to pre-emptive prevention.
Academic institutions and research centres must also be integrated into local intervention trials to evaluate the efficacy of eco-friendly larvicides and biological vector suppression tools tailored to micro-climatic zones.
Community participation remains vital to sustaining these interventions. Public awareness campaigns must empower citizens to inspect their surroundings, eliminate standing water, dispose of water-retaining trash, and neutralize mosquito breeding sites around homes.
However, civic responsibility must not serve as an excuse for institutional inaction. Local municipal authorities bear the primary obligation to ensure reliable solid waste collection, maintain open drainage canals, prevent waterlogging, and enforce environmental compliance across urban construction projects.
Controlling dengue demands a departure from fragmented, seasonal measures in favour of a long-term, science-driven, and accountable national strategy.
Clinical preparedness must be balanced with environmental management, integrated surveillance, and robust inter-ministerial coordination.
Ultimately, the success of national dengue control must not be measured by how many hospital beds are arranged to treat the sick, but by how many infections are prevented, how many vector breeding sites are permanently eliminated, and how many lives are protected.
Without a structural transition to a One Health paradigm, Bangladesh will remain trapped in a recurring cycle of preventable loss of life and severe economic strain year after year.
Professor Dr KBM Saiful Islam is the former Dean of the Faculty of Animal Science & Veterinary Medicine and former Chairman of the Department of Medicine & Public Health at Sher‑e‑Bangla Agricultural University. He previously served as a member of the National Coordination Committee of One Health Bangladesh.

item.title: A major political test. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The standoff over the appointment of the vice-chancellor (VC) of Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) has become more than an administrative dispute. It raises serious questions about the authority of university administrations, the dignity of academics, the limits of student protest, and the present government’s ability to implement its decisions.
If a VC is prevented from entering his workplace for weeks, and if reports that his electricity and water connections were cut are substantiated, the matter goes beyond ordinary campus dissent.
A university cannot function properly if administrative decisions are challenged through prolonged blockades rather than transparent institutional procedures.
The allegations deserve scrutiny, and the university community deserves a clear account of what has happened.
Dr Sheikh Shariful Islam was appointed VC by an order issued in the name of the president and went to CUET to assume his responsibilities. He is also a former student of the university. His appointment can be questioned, and students have every right to demand transparency.
However, if there are specific allegations against him, they should be made public and examined through appropriate procedures. Preventing an administrator from entering his workplace is not a substitute for evidence, due process, or accountability.
One of the most striking aspects of the controversy is that the previous VC, Dr Sayem, whose reinstatement is reportedly being demanded by protesters, was also appointed by the BNP government.
Why, then, is one appointment accepted while the other has triggered such prolonged resistance?
The difference may have an explanation, but it should be stated clearly and supported by evidence.
If the objection concerns administrative performance, protesters should identify the specific failures. If it concerns irregularities in the appointment process, evidence should be presented.
If the dispute is rooted in political affiliations or rival interests on campus, that too should be examined openly. Questions have been raised about the former VC’s political associations and alleged closeness to a particular political group.
Such claims should be investigated impartially, not treated as established facts. The same standards must apply to both the former and current administrations.
There is also a broader concern: Whether any political group is using the banner of ordinary students to advance its own interests.
That is a legitimate question in a politically-contested campus environment, but it cannot be answered by speculation or labels. Credible evidence is needed.
Student movements can be genuine expressions of grievance while also being vulnerable to political influence. Recognizing that possibility should lead to scrutiny, not assumptions about every participant.
The reported length of the standoff raises another difficult question. Why has a VC who reportedly served for only 56 days become the focus of such an intense confrontation?
What specific grievances have made a prolonged blockade necessary, and why have those grievances not been resolved through a transparent process?
The number of days served does not, by itself, prove that the protest is unjustified. It does, however, make a clear explanation of the dispute all the more important.
The government should not dismiss student concerns simply because an appointment was made under its authority. Nor should it allow pressure alone to determine whether an appointed official can perform his duties.
These principles are compatible: Investigate credible complaints, publish findings where appropriate, protect peaceful protest, and ensure that campus administration can function under established rules.
This is why CUET has become a political test for the government. If prolonged blockades are allowed to become an effective way of forcing administrative decisions, similar confrontations could emerge at other public universities.
The risk is not that every campus will repeat the same events, but that groups elsewhere may conclude that sustained pressure is more effective than formal complaints and institutional procedures.
The government’s responsibility is therefore twofold. It must provide students with a fair and credible channel to raise concerns, while also protecting the right of university officials to carry out their lawful responsibilities.
If the appointment process was flawed, the government should address that through the proper process. If allegations against the VC are not substantiated, it should explain why the appointment stands and take lawful steps to restore normal university operations. Neither force without scrutiny nor concession without evidence will resolve the underlying problem.
Universities should not be controlled by any political party, and no administration should be immune from criticism. But neither should a group be able to claim a veto over institutional decisions by keeping a campus in deadlock.
Academic freedom includes the freedom to question authority; it also depends on rules that protect students, teachers, and administrators from coercion.
The CUET controversy is about more than one appointment. It asks whether public universities in Bangladesh will be governed through evidence, institutional rules, and accountability, or whether administrative decisions will increasingly be shaped by blockades and organized pressure. The government’s response will help determine which precedent is set.
A credible investigation, transparent communication, and a lawful resolution are the way forward. The government must demonstrate that it can uphold institutional rules without suppressing legitimate dissent.
That is the real test. Not whether the government can win a confrontation, but whether it can ensure that universities remain places where disputes are resolved through evidence and due process rather than intimidation.
SK Arman Hossain is a policy analyst and a graduate student of public policy at the University of Erfurt, Germany. Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: Maaz Sadaqat sets sights on 2027 World Cup after ODI snub. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Maaz Sadaqat may have missed out on selection for Pakistan’s upcoming One-day International (ODI) tri-series featuring England and Sri Lanka, but the swashbuckling left-hander has his sights firmly set on next year’s World Cup.

The 21-year-old made a strong impression on the international stage in the recently concluded three-match T20I series against Sri Lanka, scoring consecutive half-centuries in the first two matches to help Pakistan clinch the series.

His performances were more than just individual milestones, signalling a shift towards a more aggressive batting approach in T20 cricket, with Maaz emerging as a key figure in the change.

He scored 50 off 29 balls in the opening match, helping Pakistan recover from an underwhelming powerplay alongside captain Sahibzada Farhan.

In the second T20I, Maaz took the attack to the Sri Lankan bowlers, smashing 96 off 51 balls, including seven sixes and six fours, to come close to a maiden international century.

His impressive run, however, will have to wait for another opportunity to continue in Pakistan colours, with the batter left out of the ODI squad despite having featured in six matches in the format, including his debut, earlier this year.

Maaz had made an immediate impact in only his second ODI against Bangladesh, scoring 75 and taking three wickets with his left-arm spin. However, he struggled to maintain that form in the subsequent home series against Australia in May-June, managing scores of eight, zero and 27 on difficult surfaces.

The reasons behind his omission from the squad for the upcoming tri-series remain unclear. The break, however, offers him an opportunity to refine his game with the 2027 World Cup in mind.

“I am targeting the ODI World Cup and I am preparing for it,” Maaz said in a video interview released by the Pakistan Cricket Board on Thursday. “I have a 15-20-day window coming up which I am going to dedicate to working on myself for the World Cup.”

The youngster, who rose from tape-ball cricket in Peshawar to become a franchise T20 sensation, has continued to build his reputation on the domestic and international circuits. He also struck two centuries in the recently concluded Caribbean Premier League season.

Maaz believes the key to his progress lies in strengthening his natural game rather than focusing excessively on his weaknesses.

“[In training] I try to work as much as I can on my strengths and less on my weaknesses, because if the ball is out of my range, I’d still be able to push it for a single or two,” he said. “However, if it is in my range, then I can hit it for six with my eyes closed.

“If you watch both my CPL and international knocks, I keep a positive intent from the very start.

“And if the ball comes in my range then I don’t spare it. And when a ball is a bit here or there, I try to rotate the strike.”

That clarity of approach also extends to his preferred batting position. Although Maaz has previously said he is open to batting anywhere in the order, he admits he is most comfortable opening the innings.

“I feel the most comfortable playing as an opener,” he said.

A place in Pakistan’s squad for the 2027 World Cup would put Maaz in contention for an opening slot alongside Saim Ayub, who is averaging nearly 47, and experienced campaigner Fakhar Zaman.

Maaz, however, views the competition for places as a challenge rather than a setback.

“Even if I am asked to bat lower in the order, I’ll try to bat so well that they [team management] are forced to push me higher,” he said.

item.description:
West Indies captain Shai Hope is worried he may have to fork out excess baggage fees after picking up his third Player of the Match award on their tour of India.

The opener’s unbeaten 102 in the fourth Twenty20 International on Wednesday set up a series-levelling win in Hyderabad. He also smashed a century in the second T20 in Ranchi.

Hope has been in sizzling form throughout the tour, hitting two hundreds in the earlier One-Day International leg. And while he was pleased with his performances he said he was struggling to fit his awards in his luggage.

“To be honest, they are a bit heavy, and we have got to look at the luggage weight,” he quipped after West Indies prevailed by 24 runs.

“I think we are going to have some problems going back home.” Hope said getting off to a good start in Hyderabad was key.

“We got 50-plus opening partnership,” he added. “So it was good for us to start innings and then obviously we got that foundation, you can express yourself a bit more in the middle period and then try to give the team the best finish as could as possible.” Hope clobbered nine sixes in his 50-ball knock and drew the admiration of his opponents.

“We need to respect what he has been doing,” India opener Sanju Samson said. “He has been playing some really good cricketing shots, not taking that much risk, and respecting the bowlers as well.” Hope will look to give himself more baggage problems in Saturday’s series decider in Bengaluru.

West Indies will next visit Bangladesh for a two-test series later this month. The hosts will breathe easier knowing Hope is being rested ahead of ODI World Cup qualifiers in February.

item.title: Addressing our plastic crisis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s decision to launch a national platform to tackle plastic pollution is a welcome step towards addressing one of the country’s most persistent environmental challenges.
However, its success will depend on whether we see real commitment to concrete action rather than it becoming another initiative that produces discussions without meaningful results.
Plastic pollution has become an increasingly visible threat across Bangladesh, with plastic waste continuing to damage ecosystems and threaten public health. Excessive reliance on single-use plastics, poor waste management, and inadequate recycling facilities have allowed the problem to grow.
The consequences affect everyone -- particularly communities whose livelihoods depend on healthy waterways and a clean environment.
Bringing together government agencies, businesses, development partners, and civil society can therefore help improve coordination and promote a circular economy.
However, consumers cannot be expected to shoulder the responsibility alone. Manufacturers, importers, and brand owners must also be held accountable for the waste generated by their products.
The government must establish clear targets for reducing plastic use, expanding recycling, and improving waste collection. Existing regulations must be enforced consistently, with meaningful penalties for non-compliance. Businesses should be encouraged to reduce unnecessary packaging and invest in reusable alternatives.
Without effective monitoring, even well-intentioned policies will struggle to deliver lasting change.
Waste collectors, sorters and recyclers also have a role to play. Many work in unsafe conditions without adequate protection or recognition, and improving their working conditions and integrating them into formal waste management systems would strengthen the country’s recycling capacity.
Public awareness must be prioritized, along with adequate collection facilities and stronger enforcement. Local authorities need sufficient resources to manage waste effectively, while households and businesses must have accessible disposal options.
This platform presents an opportunity to coordinate efforts and establish accountability across sectors. Its success must include reduced plastic waste, higher recycling rates, and cleaner rivers and neighbourhoods.
Bangladesh cannot afford another initiative that exists only on paper.

item.title: Rural women have shaped our country. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The International Day of Rural Women, observed today, is an opportunity to recognize the contributions of women to rural communities -- especially in Bangladesh, where recognition remains far removed from their lived reality.
Despite their contributions to agriculture, household economies, and community life, rural women continue to be marginalized, with limited access to resources, opportunities, and decision-making.
Women play a significant role in Bangladesh’s agricultural sector -- yet female farmers often remain invisible in a system that frequently acknowledges men as the primary agricultural workers. Their labour is undervalued, and many lack ownership of the land they cultivate.
Without land titles, access to institutional credit, quality seeds, modern equipment, and agricultural training, they are left at a disadvantage despite their essential contributions to food security.
This inequality extends beyond farming: Rural women often face barriers to education, healthcare, formal employment, and financial services.
For women in climate-vulnerable areas, floods, cyclones, and river erosion add another layer of insecurity, threatening livelihoods and increasing the burden of keeping families afloat.
Addressing these challenges requires more than celebrating women once a year. Female farmers must be formally recognized in agricultural policies and included in training programs, subsidies, and credit schemes.
Ensuring women's access to land ownership and inheritance rights is equally important. Local government institutions must also create opportunities for rural women to participate meaningfully in decisions that affect their lives.
Furthermore, investments in rural education, healthcare, childcare, and safe employment can help women move beyond economic dependence. Support for women-led cooperatives and small businesses would also help create sustainable livelihoods.
Bangladesh cannot achieve inclusive development while a substantial part of its rural workforce remains overlooked. Rural women are active contributors to our economic development, and their labour must be valued, their rights protected, and their voices heard.
The true measure of this day will be whether recognition translates into lasting changes in their everyday lives.

item.title: Inside the collapse of education in the Rohingya camps. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Abdur Rashid keeps returning to the same subtraction.
He teaches at a learning centre inside Kutupalong Registered Camp , the settlement where he grew up after his family fled Myanmar, and the number he cannot make work is his own paycheck.
“I am not earning any fixed amount of salary from this community-led school. My earnings depend on the payment possible to gather from different families in this camp,” Rashid says.
“If I could teach at any learning centres under a donor-funded learning program, I might earn a stipend of around Tk 13,000 for teaching as a volunteer,” he said, describing the opportunity he lost.
Many Rohingya teachers like him have had to face this reality in Cox’s Bazar since 2025.
Rashid finished his primary schooling in camp, then pushed through years of paperwork and travel restrictions to earn a bachelor’s degree from local colleges in Cox’s Bazar.
Now, he is managing a community-led school that Rohingya families increasingly treat as their only dependable option.
He is careful not to call this progress.
“When formal donor funding began to falter, educated community members stepped forward to keep our children learning,” he says.
“That stepping-in comes at a cost that families absorb directly, rather than through an aid budget.”
Families in his network pay roughly $0.50 to $6.50 a month to keep whiteboards, markers, and modest teacher stipends flowing.
It is a system built out of necessity rather than design, and Rashid is one of thousands of Rohingya educators now holding it together by hand.
A system built for emergency, not permanence
When more than 730,000 Rohingya fled Myanmar’s Rakhine State in 2017, aid agencies opened temporary learning centres within months, teaching basic literacy in Burmese, English, and math.
Initially, children were taught using an informal curriculum called the Learning Competency Framework and Approach (LCFA).
This curriculum attempted to include Burmese, English, and Mathematics; many teachers recruited from the host community were entirely unequipped to teach in Burmese.
The curriculum failed to reconcile the spoken Rohingya dialect with Burmese written script, creating severe comprehension barriers for children.
Later on, the Bangladesh government and Unicef launched a Myanmar Curriculum by late 2021, expanding coverage toward all 410,000 school-age children in the camps through 3,200 learning centres.
A record 300,000 children enrolled in school in 2023-24, the first time Rohingya children of all ages were studied under one standardized curriculum. A dedicated campaign pulled 13,000 out-of-school children into classrooms.
However, this learning framework, temporary by design, was meant not to function as a real school network.
Host-community and Rohingya teachers taught children only five subjects through instruction in Burmese and English.
They progressed automatically through grades without formal examinations.
When the money stopped
The arithmetic Rashid does every month became the arithmetic of the entire humanitarian sector in June 2025.
The $300 million USAid fund in 2024 had fallen to $12m in June 2025.
By April, the humanitarian education sector had secured only $22m of its required $72m.
The cutbacks affected more than 6,400 learning centres across 33 camps, home to over 1.2 million people, pushing roughly 300,000 of the camps’ 437,000 school-age children out of classrooms.
Around 1,250 teachers lost their jobs overnight when Unicef and Save the Children suspended all donor-funded learning programs.
“When funds from major bilateral donors are reduced overnight, agencies face excruciating trade-offs. You cannot strip a family of their minimum 1,900-calorie daily food ration or shut down cholera treatment facilities.”
A knowledge management officer with Unicef Bangladesh in Cox’s Bazar, speaking confidentially, explained the rationale plainly.
“Education, while vital for long-term human development, is treated as a secondary priority during acute budget shortfalls.”
The community steps in
What replaced the closed centres was not a plan. It was families like the ones Rashid works with. They quietly rebuilt a parallel system out of tuition fees and volunteer labour.
These community-run schools now operate on something close to a private micro-school model, staffed by educators who completed their own upper-secondary schooling and teach one subject at a time.
The clearest sign that this parallel system now sees itself as permanent came in March 2026, when the newly formed Examination Board of Rohingya Refugees held its first matriculation exams, with question papers handed to Bangladesh’s Armed Police Battalion for secure delivery across camp exam centres.
Fifty three community-run schools joined the board at its founding, and the network now covers kindergarten through grade twelve with free enrolment.
It offers something the old learning centres never could: A certificate a student can actually hold onto.
A script they were never taught
Rohingya children in Myanmar were denied both Burmese literacy and any formal way to write their own language for decades.
Even a decade ago, aid workers were warning that most children were adopting Bengali instead , simply because it was more useful day-to-day than their mother tongue.
That changed in 2024, when Children on the Edge, a child rights organization, piloted mother-tongue lessons in Hanifi script across its Kutupalong and Bhasan Char classrooms, training more than 70 teachers for a program that now reaches over 6,300 children .
The Hanifi Rohingya script, developed in the 1980s and added to the Unicode standard in 2018, gave the language a modern, typeable form for the first time; it took years before any classroom actually taught it.
Even so, the shift remains marginal in light of the crisis; nearly 50 community schools teach the script at all, and most learning centres and madrasas still default to Burmese or Bengali, the languages of the systems around them rather than the language of the children inside them.
Where the mosque becomes the classroom
Many parents have expressed frustration with donor-funded learning centres, as they focus heavily on play-based learning and basic alphabet skills without offering a clear path to high school.
Parents in refugee camps prefer madrasas over donor-funded learning centres due to deep-seated cultural, structural, and operational differences. They worry that temporary frameworks will dilute traditional community values.
Religious learning in madrasas has deep roots in Rohingya communities that predate the 2017 exodus, and the camps’ network, running through neighbourhood maktabs and a formal examining body called Wifaq al-Madaris al-Arabia al-Rohingiya , has expanded quietly through years when donor-funded classrooms were closing.
Unlike the learning centres, madrasas generally do not require birth registration or other legal documentation many refugee families lack, and they are funded privately, often by donors in Saudi Arabia and Turkey rather than through the camps’ formal humanitarian architecture.
An education sector specialist who is sceptical of madrasas as a systemic fix concedes the pull is genuine.
“Madrasas are deeply embedded in the cultural landscape, but they cannot serve as a structural replacement for formal education,” the specialist said.
“They lack a standardized curriculum, formal learning outcome assessments, and recognized pathways toward higher education.”
As Cox’s Bazar nears a decade of hosting the mass influx of Rohingya refugees, the prolonged decay of primary education threatens not only the immediate welfare of children but the future stability of the entire region.
The existing learning framework currently provided to Rohingya children offers no viable long-term future.
Without funding commitment, the half-built futures of Rohingya children will remain permanently stalled in the muddy hills of Cox’s Bazar, leaving an entire generation stranded between a homeland they cannot return to and a world that has turned its back on their education.
Rashid does not need that document to know what adjustment and funding shifts look like from inside a classroom.
What thousands of teachers like him have built is not a fix for what donors walked away from. It is the measure of what remains in their hands.
Zulker Naeen is a Research Coordinator, Centre for Critical and Qualitative Studies (CQS) and Adjunct Faculty, Department of Media Studies and Journalism (MSJ), University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB).
